segments.t: The kitchen is warming up when Kostya, the bartender, comes in with news: a young woman is asking for the chef. Barinov is not in the mood. Here is the whole exchange.
Шеф, вас там какая-то девушка зовёт.
Кто она такая и что ей нужно?
Она сказала, что пришла с телевидения.
Я не хочу ни с кем говорить.
Она говорит, что дело очень важное.
У меня сейчас совершенно нет времени.
Она ждёт вас возле главного входа.
Пусть зайдёт ко мне в кабинет.
Она просила выйти на одну минуту.
Ладно, Костя, я сейчас подойду сам.
Спасибо, шеф, я передам ваши слова.
И налей мне крепкого чёрного чая.
Back through it, one line at a time.
Шеф, вас там какая-то девушка зовёт.

'Chef, some young woman is calling for you over there.' Listen to how 'some' is built from 'which' with a special ending bit on the end, so it means 'some or other': Kostya doesn't know her. Listen to how 'is calling for you' is literally 'calls you'. He speaks politely to the boss.
Кто она такая и что ей нужно?

'Who is she and what does she need?' The speaker uses 'who is she' translates literally to 'who she such', adding a touch of 'who is she anyway'. The second half is literally 'what to her needed', the usual pattern. Barinov throws two questions at once.
Она сказала, что пришла с телевидения.

'She said that she came from television.' They express 'from television' by uses a connecting word that with this ending means 'from', not 'with'. Both action words in the sentence end with the she-word past time frame ending bit because the woman is the subject.
Я не хочу ни с кем говорить.

'I do not want to talk to anyone.' The Russian phrase literally says 'with nobody not', and both negatives are required. The final word means 'to talk'. Barinov, as ever, would rather shout than talk.
Она говорит, что дело очень важное.

'She says that the matter is very important.' When they say 'matter' can also mean 'business', and is used in the common When they say 'what's the matter'. When they say 'important' takes a it-word ending to match it. Kostya is trying to persuade the chef without saying so.
У меня сейчас совершенно нет времени.

'I currently have absolutely no time.' Notice the part 'I have no time' translates literally to 'at me no of time'. Notice the part 'time' takes a special form after Notice the part 'no', an odd change worth learning. The word before it means 'absolutely'.
Она ждёт вас возле главного входа.

'She is waiting for you near the main entrance.' In Russian, 'is waiting for you' translates translates literally to 'waits you', with no 'for'. In Russian, 'entrance' translates is literally 'the going in', built from the connecting In Russian, 'in' translates. Both words for 'main entrance' change their endings after the connecting In Russian, 'near' translates.
Пусть зайдёт ко мне в кабинет.

'Let her come into my office.' The first word plus a future action word gives 'let her' or 'let him', and the action word already tells you it is one person. Here, 'to my' shows translates literally to 'to me', but here means 'to my place'. The final word means a private office or study.
Она просила выйти на одну минуту.

'She asked you to come out for one minute.' The way to express 'for one minute' uses a specific connecting word to say how long. The action The way to express 'come out' is the opposite of the action The way to express 'go in'.
Ладно, Костя, я сейчас подойду сам.

'Fine, Kostya, I will come over myself now.' The action 'I will come over' is used here means to come up to someone, using a specific starting bit. The last word means 'myself'. The easy opening 'fine' is used here gives away that he is curious.
Спасибо, шеф, я передам ваши слова.

'Thank you, chef, I will convey your words.' The action Listen to how 'I will convey' translates literally to 'give across', the same word Barinov used to pass on messages to Tanya. Kostya uses the polite, multiple form for 'your'.
И налей мне крепкого чёрного чая.

'And pour me some strong black tea.' The speaker uses 'tea' has that 'some of' ending, meaning 'some tea'. The speaker uses 'strong' when used for tea also means 'firm'. The action The speaker uses 'pour' is said to one person.

'Of course, chef, I will do it right now.' They express 'right now' by literally says 'straight now'. The action word means 'I will do'. Kostya agrees at once, and the scene closes as politely as it began. Here it all is again, without interruption.
Шеф, вас там какая-то девушка зовёт.
Кто она такая и что ей нужно?
Она сказала, что пришла с телевидения.
Я не хочу ни с кем говорить.
Она говорит, что дело очень важное.
У меня сейчас совершенно нет времени.
Она ждёт вас возле главного входа.
Пусть зайдёт ко мне в кабинет.
Она просила выйти на одну минуту.
Ладно, Костя, я сейчас подойду сам.
Спасибо, шеф, я передам ваши слова.
И налей мне крепкого чёрного чая.
In the end Barinov agrees to go out and see who she is. He wants his tea first, which is typical. More soon.
